Triggers.value: Other people expressing anger, even calmly

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it

Negative Appraisals.value: I have permanently changed for the worse
I will never be able to feel normal emotions again

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The profile otherwise reflects fear, vigilance, avoidance of proximity/anger cues, and beliefs that others may harm her. In that context, endorsing risky or self-endangering behavior is hard to reconcile clinically, especially with no Maladaptive Strategies items or other disinhibition/externalising content to support it.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: For intimate partner physical abuse, a global appraisal that 'you can never know who will harm you' is possible but sits somewhat awkwardly beside highly specific interpersonal triggers (physical proximity, others' anger) and trauma-linked memory content. It implies diffuse unpredictability of all potential perpetrators rather than the more coherent expected pattern of threat from close others or angry interpersonal situations.

vignette: Eleanor Okeke adjusted the heavy silk of her campaign blazer as a donor leaned in too close during the state capitol's evening reception, his elbow brushing her arm. Forty-two years prior, in a drafty legislative campaign office, that same uninvited closeness had preceded the shatter of a whiskey glass and the blunt force of a fist against her temple. She had lain on the linoleum afterward, watching a dark pool of blood creep toward her wrist while her former partner's voice dropped to a quiet, controlled steady that somehow carried more menace than shouting. Decades later, that specific convergence of closeness and controlled anger still acted as a key in a rusted lock. When that same proximity and the sight of blood occurred, they did not merely remind her of the past; they directly jolted her nervous system into a state of high alert. Her shoulders would hike, her pulse would hammer, and what frightened her most was the cold dread that would settle in her chest, convincing her that danger was already in the room. The physical jolt of the trigger did not just spike her heart rate; it directly pulled the fragmented shards of that old kitchen floor back into her periphery, forcing incomplete memories to surface. That sudden, involuntary recall cemented her conviction that she had permanently changed for the worse, losing the ordinary warmth she once took for granted. This self-imposed belief that she was fundamentally broken then kept her hyper-vigilant. Walking through the marble corridors of the legislature, she constantly scanned doorways and checked behind her as she turned corners, her entrenched mistrust making her interpret every neutral interaction as a potential threat. The incomplete picture she carried of that night directly fueled the cold dread that kept her jumpy and scanning the room. Because she could never remember the event fully, her attention fixated obsessively on proximity cues, mistaking ordinary closeness for the beginning of violence. The guilt she felt when pieces did surface then hardened her appraisal that she was permanently damaged and would never be able to feel normal emotions again. She had come to believe that this fractured recall meant her mind was deliberately pushing the memory away before she could fully recall it, and that same distorted self-view recalibrated her nervous system so that every mild expression of anger or any person stepping near her felt like an immediate provocation. Her husband's gentle reminders to rest only amplified her isolation, as she interpreted his concern as a loss of control rather than care. The cycle tightened as her threat symptoms fed back into her memories and appraisals. Because she spent the night lying awake, listening to every floorboard and strain in the old Victorian house she shared with her husband, her mind remained too scattered to process the past trauma accurately. The night vigilance ensured that when she did try to remember, the images remained disjointed and heavy with guilt. The jolt of being startled confirmed her appraisal that her nervous system was permanently damaged, which then heightened her sensitivity to anger, making her bristle at the slightest tone shift in a colleague's voice. She was certain that her avoidance was the only thing keeping her safe, so she stopped attending evening fundraises, then skipped committee briefings, until the gap in her attendance drew the attention of her party leaders. What finally brought her to Dr. Aris's office was not just the insomnia or the way her hands trembled when a reporter raised their voice, but the terrifying realization that she was building a cage out of every avoidance strategy. She hoped to break the loop that had kept her trapped for decades, even as she feared that reaching out might only prove her worst belief true: that she was permanently changed and entirely alone in it.
